# Summary: Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman, born on March 16, 1953, in New York City to a Jewish family, developed an early interest in computers, programming initially at IBM and later at MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He attended Harvard University, excelling in mathematics and physics, but left graduate school to focus on programming. At MIT, Stallman became a prominent hacker, known for his strong advocacy of unrestricted access to software source code and opposition to proprietary software restrictions. His early work included programming projects such as TECO, Emacs, and contributions to Lisp machine operating systems.
In response to increasing software restrictions in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Stallman initiated the GNU Project in 1983 with the goal of creating a free Unix-compatible operating system. He founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to support this mission and introduced the concept of copyleft licensing to protect software freedoms, exemplified in the GNU General Public License (GPL). Stallman developed key GNU tools such as GNU Emacs, GCC, GDB, and GNU Make, though the system lacked a kernel until Linux was incorporated. He advocates for naming the combined system GNU/Linux to recognize GNU’s role.
Stallman is a staunch free software activist who critiques proprietary software, digital rights management (DRM), software patents, and pervasive surveillance technologies. He is known for emphasizing the importance of terminology, preferring "free software" over "open source," and calling for phrases such as GNU/Linux. His activism extends to opposing government and corporate surveillance, refusing to use smartphones, and advocating software freedom as a moral imperative. He has been a controversial figure due to his uncompromising stances and public statements, leading to resignation from MIT and FSF leadership in 2019; however, he later returned to the FSF board in 2021 amid divided community response. Stallman continues to promote software freedom principles as head of the GNU Project.
